articles.title: How I made SVG avatars byte-identical on server and client
articles.description: Seeded avatars for React, Vue, Svelte, Angular and Web Components. The PRNG, the ID scheme and the 4,000-checksum test that keep them from ever changing.
articles.body_html:
Open the member list in almost any app. Most people never upload a photo, so you see a column of identical grey silhouettes.

The usual fixes each come with a catch:

  • Initials work until two people are both "JS". And white letters on bright tiles often fail contrast.
  • Random colors change on every render, unless you add a database column to store them.
  • Generated avatars are the right idea, but many use Math.random() or hard-coded SVG IDs. Then the server draws one face, the browser draws another, and your console fills with hydration warnings.

I wanted avatars I would never have to think about again. Same input, same bytes, on every server, in every browser and in every release. That became Opaline. This post covers what it gives you, how to use it, and the engineering that makes the promise hold.

Why you might want it

You want What Opaline does
Users you can tell apart Each seed gets its own face, colors and shape. Five styles.
Avatars that never change Same seed and options give a byte-identical SVG for all of 1.x, checked in CI
No hydration warnings Server and client produce the same markup. Tested in Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit and Angular SSR.
One library across your stack One core and components for React 18+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.20+, Angular 20–22, plus a Web Component
A small bundle Core is 1.27 kB gzipped with zero dependencies. With the largest style it's 5.57 kB.
Photos when users have them Pass src. If it's missing or broken, the generated face stays.
Brand colors and dark mode Colors are CSS variables, so you restyle without regenerating
Accessible initials Letters clear WCAG AA (4.5:1) on every palette, checked for 2,100 seed/palette pairs
No license review MIT for the code and the art

Using it

Install the package for your framework. Each one pulls in the core.

npm i @inlaylab/opaline-react   # or -vue, -svelte, -angular, -element

React (server-component safe, React 18 or later):

import { Avatar, AvatarGroup } from '@inlaylab/opaline-react'
import { clay } from '@inlaylab/opaline/clay'

<Avatar seed={user.email} look={clay} src={user.photo} alt={user.name} />
<AvatarGroup look={clay} members={team.map((u) => u.email)} max={4} alt="Project members" />

Vue 3.5+ / Nuxt:

<Avatar :seed="user.email" :look="clay" :src="user.photo" :alt="user.name" />

Svelte 5.20+ / SvelteKit:

<Avatar seed={user.email} look={clay} src={user.photo} alt={user.name} />

Angular 20–22 (standalone, OnPush, works zoneless):

<op-avatar [seed]="email" [look]="clay" [src]="photo" alt="Ada" />

No framework:

<script type="module">import '@inlaylab/opaline-element'</script>
<opaline-avatar seed="ada@inlay.dev" look="clay" finish="gloss" size="64" alt="Ada"></opaline-avatar>

No DOM at all. createAvatar returns a plain string, so it works in an API route, a build script or an email template:

import { createAvatar } from '@inlaylab/opaline'
import { clay } from '@inlaylab/opaline/clay'

const { svg } = createAvatar(clay, { seed: 'ada@inlay.dev', body: 'hood', ears: 'bunny' })

Any option you set pins that part of the avatar. The seed fills in the rest.

Need a PNG for an OG card, a push notification or a profile-photo upload? toPng (688 B) does it in the browser with no dependencies:

import { toPng } from '@inlaylab/opaline/png'
const blob = await toPng(createAvatar(clay, { seed }), { size: 512 })

Now the interesting part: how "same bytes everywhere" actually holds.

1. The seed is the only input, so normalize it first

Users type Ada@Inlay.dev with a trailing space on one form and ada@inlay.dev on another. If those give different faces, you get a bug report. So every seed goes through this first:

const EMAIL = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+$/

export function normalizeSeed(seed: string | number | null | undefined): string {
  const s = String(seed ?? '').trim().normalize('NFC')
  return EMAIL.test(s) ? s.toLowerCase() : s
}

NFC matters more than it looks. Zoë can arrive as one code point (ë) or two (e plus a combining diaeresis), depending on the OS and keyboard. Without NFC those are two different people.

Only emails are lower-cased. Usernames like Ada and ada can be different accounts, so they keep their case.

2. No Math.random(): a seeded PRNG with forks

The seed goes through xmur3, a small string hash, which seeds sfc32, a fast 32-bit PRNG. Both fit in a few lines and give identical results on every JavaScript engine, because they use only Math.imul, shifts and | 0:

export function createRng(seed: string): Rng {
  const h = xmur3(seed)
  const next = sfc32(h(), h(), h(), h())
  // Early sfc32 outputs are weakly mixed; skip them.
  for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++) next()
  // ...
  return {
    next, float, int, pick,
    // A fork depends only on the seed and label, never on earlier draws.
    fork: (label) => createRng(seed + '\u0000' + label),
  }
}

The fork line is the most important decision in the library.

A naive generator draws everything from one stream: shape, then color, then eyes, then mouth. Now add a new eyebrow option in a later release. It takes one draw from the stream, and every draw after it shifts. Every existing user's mouth changes. That's a breaking change you didn't mean to ship.

With forks, each feature gets its own stream, keyed by the seed and a label:

const g = rng.fork('color')
const hue = g.pick(palette.hues) + g.float(-9, 9)

fork('color') gives the same numbers whether it's called first or last, or after ten new features. New features get new labels. Old faces never move.

The \u0000 separator stops a seed of "ab" with label "c" from colliding with seed "a" and label "bc".

3. SVG IDs that are unique per page and identical across hydration

SVG gradients and filters need ids. That creates two separate bugs:

  1. Two avatars on one page share id="grad". The second one silently uses the first one's gradient, so the wrong colors appear.
  2. The server and the client invent different IDs. You get a hydration mismatch.

Opaline builds every ID from two parts:

const id = createIds(
  hash(seed + '\u0000' + style.name + '\u0000' + stableStringify(options)),
  instance,
)
// id('grad') -> "a<7-char hash>-grad-<instance>"
  • The prefix is a hash of the seed, the style and the options. The same seed with different options never shares <defs>. stableStringify sorts the keys, so option order never matters.
  • The instance suffix comes from each framework's SSR-safe ID primitive:
Package Instance from Minimum version
React useId() React 18, the version that introduced useId
Vue useId() Vue 3.5. Multiple apps on a page set app.config.idPrefix.
Svelte $props.id() Svelte 5.20
Angular An injectable per-app counter. Server and client render in the same order, so the numbers match. Angular 20
Web Component A module counter. There is no SSR, so only uniqueness matters. Any modern browser

That table is also why the minimum versions are what they are. 1.1.2 lowered React to 18 for exactly this reason: useId exists there, so nothing else was blocking it.

4. Defaults are invisible

One rule turned out to matter a lot: an option set to its default must give byte-for-byte the same output as leaving it unset.

Without that rule, <Avatar finish="soft"> and <Avatar> hash to different ID prefixes, so a refactor that spells out a default changes your markup. Each style declares its defaults, and createAvatar drops matching values before hashing:

for (const k in defaults)
  if (rest[k] === defaults[k]) delete rest[k]

stableStringify also skips undefined values. Wrappers pass every prop through, and { shape: undefined } must not hash differently from {}.

Proof, not promises

"Deterministic" is an easy word to write in a README. Here is how the repo checks it.

A frozen checksum file: 4,000 hashes

frozen-1.json holds 4,000 SHA-256 digests (first 16 hex characters):

  • 100 seeds shaped like real input: emails, Person B12-style names, base36 IDs, plain numbers, and Unicode with emoji (Zoë Nguyễn 4 😀).
  • 40 option sets across all five styles: every finish, every shape, palettes, hood and ears, custom initials text. 
test(`1.x output is frozen: ${key}`, () => {
  const now = FROZEN_SEEDS.map((seed) => digest(createAvatar(style, { ...opts, seed }).svg))
  const changed = FROZEN_SEEDS.filter((_, i) => now[i] !== manifest[key]?.[i])
  expect(changed, `Output changed for ${key}...`).toEqual([])
})

If one byte of one avatar changes, CI fails and names the seed. A second test checks that the manifest still covers every case, so nobody can make the guarantee pass by deleting rows. The only way to change the output is to regenerate the file on purpose, and that means a major version.

That's what lets you cache an avatar on a CDN forever, store the SVG in a database, or put it in an email that will be opened in three years.

Real SSR apps, hydrated in a real browser

Four sample apps live in the repo: Next (App Router, RSC), Nuxt, SvelteKit and Angular SSR (zoneless). For each one, Playwright:

  1. starts the production server and fetches the HTML;
  2. asserts that every id in the page is unique, and that the named avatar has role="img" and aria-label;
  3. loads the page in Chromium and fails on any console message matching /hydrat/i, any error and any page exception;
  4. compares the hydrated DOM with the server HTML: every avatar's root attributes and its <svg> must be exactly what the server sent.

Step 4 exists because of something I found while writing step 3. Production Svelte repairs a hydration mismatch silently. No warning, no error. The page looks fine, the console is clean, and the bug is invisible. Watching the console isn't enough. You have to diff the DOM.

Size, enforced

size-limit runs in CI with a budget for every entry point. These are today's numbers, minified and gzipped:

Import Size Budget
createAvatar (core) 1.27 kB 3 kB
core + Aura 2.52 kB 4 kB
core + Initials 2.86 kB 4 kB
core + Morph 4.90 kB 5 kB
core + Gradient 5.13 kB 5.25 kB
core + Clay 5.57 kB 8 kB
React wrapper (avatar + group) 854 B 1.5 kB
PNG export 688 B 1 kB

Styles are separate imports, so you only ship the ones you use.

Speed

A perf test builds 500 Clay avatars with the gloss finish, the heaviest combination. It warms the JIT, then keeps the best of five runs. On my laptop (Node 24) that's 56–63 ms, about 120 µs per avatar. CI fails above 250 ms, so a slow shared runner doesn't flake the build. A member list of 200 people costs you around 25 ms of CPU, once.

What broke along the way

I broke my own promise once, on purpose. 1.1.0 shipped Initials with white letters. On the brightest tiles that was as low as 1.9:1 contrast, far below the 4.5:1 that WCAG AA asks for. Shipping unreadable letters for the rest of 1.x seemed worse than changing them. So 1.1.1 changed exactly one thing: the <text> fill on non-pastel palettes is now a deep shade of the tile's own hue. Nothing else changed: no shapes, no other styles. A new test checks 300 seeds on each of the 7 palettes and fails if any pair falls below 4.5:1. The README lists this as the one deliberate exception.

useId output isn't a valid SVG ID fragment. Depending on the version, React's IDs contain characters such as : (:r1: in React 18) or «». Those characters cause trouble inside url(#…) references, so the wrapper strips everything except word characters and dashes before it uses the suffix.

undefined changed the hash. Wrappers forward every prop, so the core saw { shape: undefined } and hashed it differently from {}. The result was a different ID prefix for the same avatar, depending on which wrapper rendered it. That's why stableStringify now filters undefined values.

A silent Svelte fix hid a real mismatch, as described above. That's why the e2e diffs the DOM and doesn't trust the console.

When not to use it

  • You want dozens of art styles, or an image URL from a hosted HTTP API with no code at all: use DiceBear. It's excellent.
  • You're React-only and want minimal abstract shapes in your exact brand palette: Boring Avatars is lovely.
  • You need server-side PNG with zero setup: Opaline's forRaster() prepares the SVG, but you still bring a rasterizer such as @resvg/resvg-js.

The comparison page goes row by row, including the rows where the others win.

Try it

  • 🎨 Playground: type your own name. Every setting lives in the URL, so you can share an exact avatar.
  • ⭐ GitHub: MIT for code and art.
  • 📦 npm i @inlaylab/opaline

One question I'd really like your take on: is "byte-identical within a major version" the right contract? Or would you rather have "looks the same" and let me fix rendering details in minor releases? I went with bytes because it makes CDN caching and email trivially safe, but it does make every bug fix a judgement call.

articles.title: How I rank 250 countries for every month of the year
articles.description: Two penalties, 30 years of climate data and one Postgres query build twelve monthly rankings. Here's how it works, and which assumption matters most.
articles.body_html:
PickOH, the travel site I run, has twelve ranking pages, one per month. Where to Go in August currently lists 62 countries and territories, from Malawi at #1 to Svalbard at #62. Nobody orders them by hand. A scoring formula and one Postgres query build all twelve pages from 30 years of climate data.

This post covers how the ranking works, the bug that gave four countries the same #1, and what happened when each assumption in the formula was tested.

The data: one point per country, 30 years deep

Each of the 250 countries and territories has twelve rows in Postgres, one per month: average daily high, average daily low, total rainfall and rain days. The numbers are 1991–2020 climate normals from the ERA5 reanalysis, fetched through Open-Meteo's archive API. Each one is measured at a single location, usually the capital.

Fetching it mostly took patience: 30-year requests use up Open-Meteo's free quota quickly, so the backfill had to cache and resume per location. Auditing the result was the harder job:

  • Ten places, including Finland, Iceland and Russia, shared one identical placeholder temperature curve that peaked in April.
  • Sixteen large countries stored temperatures from the wrong region: the Sahara for Algeria, the Andes for Peru, the outback for Australia, Mumbai for India. Their rainfall and coordinates described the capital, so each row was describing two places at once.
  • Checking every remaining location against ERA5 found 32 more like that.

The fix came down to one rule: temperature, rain and coordinates must all describe the same place. Bolivia stayed as it was, because ERA5 misreads the sharp relief around La Paz and the stored curve already matched the real city.

The score

Every month of every country gets a penalty score. Lower is better, and 0 is a perfect month.

The temperature penalty is the number of degrees the average daily high sits outside 18–26°C. The rain penalty treats 25 mm of monthly rain as one degree of discomfort. A month at 30°C with 50 mm of rain scores 4 + 2 = 6.

A country's two lowest-scoring months become its picks. Exact ties go to the drier month, then the earlier one.

Why two? Jordan is a good example:

Amman is cool and damp in winter, then dry but hitting 33–36°C in summer. The good months sit between those seasons, so the picks land in October and April. A single best month would hide one of them.

That shape is common. 64 of the 250 have picks that aren't consecutive months, and for 10 of them, including China, the two picks are exactly six months apart.

Temperature alone wouldn't be enough. 135 countries have three or more months inside the band, which would leave those months tied at zero. Colombia is the extreme case: Bogotá's average high stays between 18 and 20°C all year, so rain alone picks August and September.

Two stages, not one sort

The obvious design is to sort all 250 by each month's score. The pages do something different:

  1. Qualify. A country appears on a month's page only if that month is one of its own two picks. This compares a country with itself.
  2. Order. The qualifiers are sorted by raw score. This compares countries with each other.

So August's page means "places at their best in August", not "the mildest places on Earth in August". A plain sort answers the second question, and the answer barely changes: Saint Helena would make the top ten in 11 months of the year, and every page would be 250 entries long.

Because qualifying is relative, places that are never pleasant still get two months. 92 of the 250 never have a month inside the band. Iceland peaks at 14.5°C in July, and both of Antarctica's best months are below freezing. Stage two handles them: Iceland is #52 of 60 for July, and Antarctica is #41 of 41 for December.

Both stages run in a single Postgres query per page. The same query finds each country's other pick, which becomes the "Also great in July" line on its card.

The bug: four countries at #1

The page position originally used competition ranking, where tied entries share a number. Malawi, Peru, Zambia and Zimbabwe all round to a score of 0.0 for August, so the cards read #1, #1, #1, #1, #5. The database was doing exactly what it was asked to do, and the page still looked broken.

Switching to a simple running count over the same order fixed it. The rounding stayed, so countries with effectively identical weather fall alphabetically instead of being separated by differences no traveller would notice.

One formula, three copies

Each country's Weather tab shows the same picks, with the two months marked in gold and green:

That creates a maintenance problem, because the scoring logic exists in three places:

  • TypeScript in the browser, for those Weather tab badges
  • SQL, for the month pages
  • TypeScript on the server, for the best-month text in server-rendered HTML

Comments say to change them together, and a unit test pins the key parts of the query. Neither proves they agree. So for this post, an independent Python version of the score was run on every country's twelve months from the live API and compared with all twelve ranking pages: 250 countries, 500 picks, 0 mismatches.

That check isn't in CI, which is the weak spot. A shared fixture that all three implementations have to pass would close it.

Which assumption matters most?

The 25 mm constant and the 18–26°C band are both judgement calls. To see how much each one matters, the picks were recalculated with different values, counting how many countries' top month changed:

The rain constant is stable. Moving it to 20 or 30 mm changes 2–3% of top picks, and doubling or halving it changes 7–11%. Removing rain altogether changes 21%, even with the drier month still winning ties.

The comfort band is the strongest opinion in the model. Sliding it 2°C either way changes 22–24% of top picks, and stretching the top to 30°C changes 29%. Someone planning a beach holiday would want a warmer band and would get a noticeably different list. The band is already a parameter, so a personal comfort setting wouldn't need new scoring logic.

The year isn't evenly spread

Each country gets two picks, but they don't land evenly across the calendar:

The February and August peaks come mostly from the tropics, where the dry season flips across the equator. In January and February, 89 of the 90 tropical picks come from north of the equator. By July and August, 52 of 71 come from south of it. Countries north of the tropics cluster around May and September, either side of the summer heat.

What the score can't see

  • Cloud. Peru is #2 for August: 21°C and under 1 mm of rain in Lima. The score is nearly perfect, but Lima's winter is known for grey skies and garúa, a coastal mist that barely registers as rain.
  • Humidity. Only the daily high counts, so a sticky 30°C scores the same as a dry one. Night lows and rain days appear on the cards but aren't scored.
  • Geography. One point stands in for a whole country. China's picks are Beijing's, which says nothing about tropical Hainan.
  • Grid resolution. ERA5 uses a 0.25° grid, roughly 25 km. Tokyo's stored August high is 27°C, while published climate tables put it near 30°C. At 30°C, August would drop out of Japan's top two and April would replace it.
  • Good months that miss the cut. Greece's October scores 1.10, which would place it around #7 on October's page, but it isn't listed because May and September score better. Across the year, 193 of the 408 country-months scoring 2 or better don't appear on any page. It's also why page length says little about how many good options exist: November lists 17 countries while 31 score that well, and July lists 60 while only 23 do.

The ranking has to exist in the HTML too

The month pages are React, and the browser fetches the ranking after load. Early on, curl on a month page found zero <a href> tags, so anything that didn't run JavaScript saw no ranking and no links.

The server now loads the same ranking and renders it as plain anchors in the initial HTML. Between them, the twelve pages link every country's weather page. Three details matter:

  • The server-rendered list has to match what the page shows, in the same order. Anything else is cloaking.
  • If the query fails, the page still renders without its links rather than returning an error.
  • The bare /where-to-go URL answers with a 302 and Cache-Control: no-store, because its target changes every month.

All twelve months

Here is every page, with the number of countries that qualify:

January (50) · February (65) · March (28) · April (24) · May (44) · June (36) · July (60) · August (62) · September (45) · October (28) · November (17) · December (41)

If you were adding one more term to the score, would it be cloud cover or humidity? I'd like to hear how you'd weight it.

articles.title: The Junior Developer Comeback: Seniors will struggle to get a job?
articles.description: Right now, juniors are struggling.  Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a...
articles.body_html:
Right now, juniors are struggling.

Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a data analyst, the entry-level door feels like it's closing. Seniors, on the other hand, are mostly getting hired or retained.

I think that's about to reverse. Not this year, but within the next five to ten years, I believe juniors will do very well, and seniors will be the ones fighting for jobs.

Let me explain.

Learn Git by completing missions

Why juniors are struggling right now

The current state of AI is good, but it isn't senior-level good.

It can write code, generate designs, and crunch data. But it still needs someone experienced to guide it, catch its mistakes, and make the calls that actually matter. That's exactly what a senior does.

So companies are doing the logical thing for today's reality:

  • Keep the seniors, because they can steer AI and fix what it gets wrong.
  • Skip the juniors, because AI already covers a lot of what juniors used to do.

That's the world we're in right now, and it explains why the junior market feels so rough.

What happens in 5 to 10 years?

Now fast forward.

By then, AI will probably be senior-level good. Not "impressive for a tool," but genuinely capable of senior-level work.

Here's the part that matters: someone still has to operate it.

Even with extremely capable AI, people will need some technical skill to use it well. Not a lot, but some. You need enough understanding to describe what you want, to judge whether the output is right, and to know when something is off.

And not everyone will have that.

Most people won't have spent time learning graphic design, web development, or data analysis. The people who did will have a real edge, because they understand the fundamentals well enough to operate the AI properly.

The incentive to hire seniors disappears

This is where the economics flip.

Picture two candidates:

Senior Junior (with some technical skill)
Output with senior-level AI Great Just as great
Salary expectation High Much lower

If AI closes the gap in raw capability, then the senior's main advantage, years of hard-won technical expertise, matters a lot less. The junior with a bit of technical knowledge gets the same job done just as well.

The senior costs more and delivers about the same result.

From a business perspective, the decision becomes easy. Why pay more for a result you can get for less? The incentive to hire a senior drops, and hiring a junior with some technical knowledge starts to make far more sense.

Where I could be wrong

I don't want to pretend this is a certainty. A few things could change the picture:

  • Seniors might shift their value. If the gap in technical execution disappears, seniors could compete on things AI doesn't replace, like judgment, product sense, communication, and owning the consequences when something breaks.
  • "A little technical skill" might not be enough. If AI makes mistakes that are subtle or expensive, companies may still pay for deep expertise as insurance.
  • Timelines are uncertain. Five to ten years is a guess, and AI progress has surprised people in both directions.
  • The pipeline problem. If nobody hires juniors for years, fewer people will build the technical foundation that this whole argument depends on.

Even so, I think the core pressure is real: when capability gets cheap, the premium for experience shrinks.

What this means for you

If you're a junior: Don't give up on learning the fundamentals. The market is hard right now, but the technical foundation you build is the thing that could set you apart later. Learn the craft, and learn to work with AI, not against it.

If you're a senior: Don't rely on years of experience alone. Lean into what's hardest to automate, such as decision-making, system thinking, and being the person who can be trusted with outcomes, not just output.

Final thoughts

Today's market rewards seniors because AI isn't senior-level yet. Tomorrow's market might reward cheaper people who can operate a senior-level AI.

The people who win won't necessarily be the most experienced. They'll be the ones who have just enough technical skill to get the most out of the tools.

I could be completely off, so I'd love to hear what you think.

Do you think juniors will bounce back once AI reaches senior-level ability, or will seniors always have the upper hand? Let me know in the comments. 👇

articles.title: When did you last code a project fully by hand ?
articles.description: Recently I attended my first AI meetup in my city  and I loved it really loved it. I walked out with...
articles.body_html:
Recently I attended my first AI meetup in my city and I loved it really loved it. I walked out with an idea for a new project and this time, instead of reaching for Cursor or any other AI assistant tool, I opened VS Code and Google and decided to read blogs and implement whatever I didn't understand.

Seems legit, right?

Nope.

As soon as I sat down to code I went completely blank. I couldn't write basic boilerplate for Node.js. In the file below, I was using Express and forgot to pass the PORT to listen(). I was passing / instead of PORT. 😭

It turns out I hadn't written code by hand in about 3 months. The scary part was that I could read code understand it and even spot mistakes in it but when it was my turn to write it, my hands froze.

Errors I Got

1. MongoDB wasn't connecting. I checked the logs and saw this:

MongoParseError: Invalid scheme, expected connection string to start with "mongodb://" or "mongodb+srv://"

But my URL already started with that so my instinct said to paste the error into AI and get the root cause but hey, we made a rule so I went to Google instead.

At first I thought the fix was wrapping the value in String(), but that only silences TypeScript's "could be undefined" warning.

The real problem was that I had put my .env file inside src instead of the project root (the server folder). dotenv never found it, so process.env.MONGO_DB_URL was undefined, and Mongoose was literally being handed the word "undefined". Moving the .env to the root fixed it.

Lesson: when you see an "invalid connection string" error, don't trust your URL, check whether the variable is even being loaded.

2. My IP address wasnt being accepted. I was like, why?? After 10 minutes I remembered I was on a VPN when I created the cluster so Atlas had saved the VPN's IP in Network Access. I had to add my actual IP address.

The Temptation

The urge to open Cursor, get the project done, deploy it and move on was strong. But then I asked myself a few questions:

Is this project going to make me money? (Right now, no.)
Is it under a strict deadline? (No.)
Am I chasing speed even though I can afford to be slow?

So... why the rush?

What I Did Instead

I resisted the urge. I googled everything, relearned (or rather, remembered) the syntax and wrote every line by hand.

And honestly? It felt great. I felt like one of those hackers in the movies. I was on cloud nine, and I loved that feeling.

Takeaway

AI has genuinely changed how we work. Boilerplate, syntax and repetitive setup, the stuff that used to eat hours, can now be done in seconds. That means developers can spend more of their energy on what actually matters: business logic, system design, architecture decisions and solving real problems for real users. Knowing what to build and why is becoming more valuable than remembering how to type it.

But this experience showed me the other side of the coin. When you hand off every line to a tool you slowly lose the muscle memory that makes you fast, confident and independent.

I could read the code and spot the bugs but I couldn't write it from scratch. Understanding and recall are two different skills, and only one of them comes from watching.

So heres where I've landed. Use AI for speed when the deadline is real and the stakes are high, but when theres no rush, build something by hand once in a while.

Struggle through the docs, make the silly mistakes (like forgetting the PORT 😅) and fix them yourself. It keeps your fundamentals sharp and honestly it brings back the dopamine that shipping with a single prompt never quite gives you.

When did you last build a project fully by hand?

articles.title: Turning a video clip into a game sprite sheet in the browser
articles.description: I make 2D characters by generating a short animation video and cutting it into a sprite sheet. For a...
articles.body_html:
I make 2D characters by generating a short animation video and cutting it into a sprite sheet. For a while that meant ffmpeg, a Python script and a lot of fiddling with transparency. I moved the whole thing into a browser page so it runs on the user's machine and the video never leaves it. This post is what I learned along the way: reading frames from a <video>, removing a flat backdrop from compressed frames, and keeping the character's feet in place.


A character reference turned into an animated sprite (AI-generated with SpriteCanvas)

All code below is plain JavaScript with no dependencies.

1. Reading frames: seek, wait, draw

There is no "give me frame 37" API on HTMLVideoElement. What works everywhere is: set currentTime, wait for seeked, draw the video to a canvas, read the pixels.

// Call after the video fired 'loadeddata', so the first frame is decoded.
async function readFrames(video, times, width, height) {
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = width;
  canvas.height = height;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });
  const frames = [];
  for (const t of times) {
    if (Math.abs(video.currentTime - t) > 0.001) {
      const seeked = new Promise((resolve) => video.addEventListener('seeked', resolve, { once: true }));
      video.currentTime = t;
      await seeked;
    }
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);
    ctx.drawImage(video, 0, 0, width, height);
    frames.push(ctx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height).data);
  }
  return frames;
}

Three things bit me:

  • Don't seek to the very end. A seek to exactly video.duration often shows no frame. I keep every sample time below duration - 0.01.
  • Round the sample times. start + i / fps accumulates float error; I round to microseconds so 0.1 + 0.2 style noise doesn't skip or duplicate a frame.
  • Background tabs stall. Chrome holds back video loading and decoding in a hidden tab, so a long read just stops when the user switches tabs. Before every seek I wait until the tab is visible again: 
function whenVisible() {
  if (!document.hidden) return Promise.resolve();
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const shown = () => {
      if (document.hidden) return;
      document.removeEventListener('visibilitychange', shown);
      resolve();
    };
    document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', shown);
  });
}

I also cap the read at 512 frames and check frames × width × height × 4 bytes up front, because a 10-second 1080p clip at 30 fps is about 2.5 GB of RGBA.

requestVideoFrameCallback and WebCodecs are faster, but the first follows playback and drops frames when the page is busy, and the second needs its own demuxer. Seeking is the one path that behaves the same in Chrome, Firefox and Safari, and for a few hundred frames it is fast enough.

2. Finding the backdrop

Generated clips and green-screen recordings have a flat backdrop, so I look at the four corners. For PNG sheets I require the corners to match within 12 per channel. Video frames carry compression noise, so there I allow 24 and use the average of the corners as the key colour.

function detectBackdrop(rgba, w, h) {
  const corners = [0, (w - 1) * 4, (h - 1) * w * 4, ((h - 1) * w + w - 1) * 4];
  const first = corners[0];
  const close = (p) => [0, 1, 2].every((c) => Math.abs(rgba[p + c] - rgba[first + c]) <= 24);
  if (!corners.every(close)) return null;
  return [0, 1, 2].map((c) => Math.round(corners.reduce((sum, p) => sum + rgba[p + c], 0) / 4));
}

3. Removing it: flood fill vs. "everywhere"

For a still sprite sheet I flood-fill from the edges, so a backdrop-coloured pixel inside the character (a green gem on a green screen) survives. For video I clear every matching pixel, like a chroma key, because the gaps between arms and legs are not connected to the border in every frame, and a flood fill leaves them filled.

The hard part is the edge. A scaled, compressed video leaves a one-pixel ring of blended colour around the character: half character, half magenta. Clearing by a tolerance either leaves a pink halo or eats into the character.

What worked: for each remaining pixel that touches a cleared pixel, compare it with the pixel just inside it, the neighbour on the opposite side from the cleared one. If it sits more than halfway from that inner pixel towards the backdrop colour, it is fringe and goes. When the inner pixel is cleared too, the pixel is part of a one-pixel line, so I keep it.

// How far p is from the inner pixel q towards the backdrop colour: 0 at q, 1 at the backdrop.
function towardBackdrop(rgba, p, q, key) {
  let dot = 0, len = 0;
  for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
    const axis = key[c] - rgba[q + c];
    dot += (rgba[p + c] - rgba[q + c]) * axis;
    len += axis * axis;
  }
  return len ? dot / len : 1;
}

This is a projection onto the line between the sprite colour and the key colour, so it works for any backdrop colour and any character colour, without a per-video tolerance.

4. Trimming without losing the motion

Each video frame is mostly empty, so I crop. The trap: cropping each frame to its own bounding box makes the character jump around, because a sword swing makes the box wider in some frames. Crop every frame by the union of all the boxes instead; relative motion stays intact and the sheet is still small.

const union = boxes.reduce((u, b) => !b ? u : !u ? b : {
  x0: Math.min(u.x0, b.x0), y0: Math.min(u.y0, b.y0),
  x1: Math.max(u.x1, b.x1), y1: Math.max(u.y1, b.y1),
}, null);

There is an optional second step for clips where the camera drifts: move each frame so the bottom centre of its content lands where the first frame's does. I leave it off by default, because for a jump the feet are supposed to leave the ground.

5. The atlas

The output is one PNG in a grid plus a JSON Hash atlas, which Phaser and PixiJS load as is. Two fields matter beyond the frame rectangles:

"frames": {
  "hero-attack-03": {
    "frame": { "x": 768, "y": 0, "w": 256, "h": 256 },
    "pivot": { "x": 0.5, "y": 0.875 },
    "duration": 83
  }
}
  • pivot is the foot point, so every animation of a character stands on the same line in the engine.
  • duration is per frame in milliseconds. Phaser keeps unknown frame fields in customData and ignores duration for playback, so pass it yourself: 
const tex = this.textures.get('hero-attack');
this.anims.create({
  key: 'attack',
  frames: tex.getFrameNames().sort().map((frame) => ({
    key: 'hero-attack', frame, duration: tex.get(frame).customData?.duration,
  })),
});

(getFrameNames() has no guaranteed order; zero-padded names make .sort() enough. This is for Phaser 3.80 and later, where a frame's duration replaces the base frame time; up to 3.70 it is added on top.)

What I'd do differently

  • Ask for a flat, unusual backdrop colour (magenta) when generating the clip. Green screen fights green cloaks.
  • Ask for the last frame to match the first. Loops stop popping, and you don't have to hunt for a loop point.
  • A "breathing" idle that is just the sprite scaled up and down looks fake in the engine. Generate a real idle motion (chest, shoulders, cloth) instead. I shipped the scaled kind first and had to redo it.

The tool from this post is free and runs in the browser: video to sprite sheet. I built it as part of SpriteCanvas, which also generates the character and the animation clips; the sample art here was made with it (AI-generated).

articles.title: Your PHP API Sends Keys 10 Then 2. Your TypeScript Client Reads 2 Then 10
articles.description: PHP arrays keep insertion order. JavaScript objects list integer-like keys first, ascending. Why it happens, the array_filter twin, and the fixes.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your PHP controller builds the shipping options for a checkout dropdown. Product wants Express on top, so you build the array in that order: ['10' => 'Express', '2' => 'Standard', 'pickup' => 'Store pickup']. The JSON leaves the server with the keys in that order. The TypeScript frontend loops over it with Object.entries, and Standard renders first.

Nobody sorted anything. Both runtimes did exactly what their specs say. A PHP array remembers insertion order for every key. A JavaScript object lists integer-like keys first, in ascending numeric order, and only then the other string keys in the order they were created.

Two languages, two meanings of "in order"

The PHP manual says it in one line: "An array in PHP is actually an ordered map." Int keys and string keys share one sequence, and that sequence is insertion order until you call a sort function.

There is one wrinkle on the way in. The same page explains that strings holding valid decimal integers are cast to int: the key "8" is stored under 8, while "08" stays a string. So '10' and '2' in your literal become int keys 10 and 2. The order survives the cast.

JavaScript objects follow a different rule. The ECMAScript spec algorithm that orders an object's own keys is OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys, and it has three passes:

  1. Every own key that is an array index, "in ascending numeric index order".
  2. Every other string key, "in ascending chronological order of property creation".
  3. Every symbol key, also in creation order.

The APIs you reach for every day sit on top of that. The archived for-in order proposal lists Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries, JSON.parse and JSON.stringify as for-in-ordered APIs, and MDN's for...in page puts the rule plainly: integer keys "will be traversed first in ascending order by value, then other string keys in ascending chronological order of property creation." MDN's Object.keys page shows it with { 100: "a", 2: "b", 7: "c" }, which comes back as ['2', '7', '100'].

Is either side breaking JSON? No. RFC 8259 defines an object as "an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs" and notes that parsers "have been observed to differ as to whether or not they make the ordering of object members visible to calling software." The wire format never promised you order. PHP happened to keep it, and JavaScript applies its own rule.


Same cards, two rules: PHP keeps the line as built, a JavaScript object pulls integer-like keys to the front.

Watch it happen in PHP and Node

Here is the PHP side. Save it as order.php and run php order.php:

<?php
$options = [
    '10' => 'Express',
    '2' => 'Standard',
    'pickup' => 'Store pickup',
];

var_dump(array_keys($options));
// int 10, int 2, string "pickup": insertion order

echo json_encode($options), PHP_EOL;
// a JSON object, keys written as 10, 2, pickup

json_encode writes an object here because, in the manual's words, "if the keys are not a continuous numeric sequence starting from 0, all keys are encoded as strings, and specified explicitly for each key-value pair." Keys 10 and 2 are not a sequence from 0, so you get an object, in PHP's order.

Now the client. Save it as order.mjs and run it with Node.js:

const body =
  '{"10":"Express","2":"Standard","pickup":"Store pickup"}';
const options = JSON.parse(body);

for (const [id, label] of Object.entries(options)) {
  console.log(id, label);
}
// spec order: "2" first, then "10", then "pickup"

The text on the wire still says 10 first. The object built from it lists 2 first, because "2" and "10" are array indices and "pickup" is not. Round-trip it through JSON.stringify and the reordered version is what goes back out: MDN's JSON.stringify page says properties are visited "using the same algorithm as Object.keys()".

TypeScript cannot warn you. JSON.parse returns any, and a Record<string, string> describes both orders identically. Key order is not part of the type system.

Which keys move, exactly

The spec's definition of array index is narrower than "looks like a number". It is a key whose canonical numeric form is an integer from 0 up to 2^32 − 2. That gives you a few edge cases worth knowing:

  • "01" is not in canonical form, so it keeps creation order. PHP agrees here: per the manual, "08" stays a string key too.
  • "-1" and "1.5" are not array indices (one is negative, the other is not an integer), so they keep creation order.
  • "4294967295" (2^32 − 1) and anything larger keeps creation order.

So the reshuffle depends on the values of your keys. A map keyed by small auto-increment IDs gets sorted. The same map keyed by slugs or 64-bit snowflake IDs keeps its order. One endpoint can behave differently in staging and production because the data is different.

The sibling trap: array_filter turns a list into an object

The same rule in json_encode causes a second bug, and this one breaks code instead of reordering it. array_filter does not renumber: "Array keys are preserved, and may result in gaps if the array was indexed." A list with a gap is no longer a continuous sequence from 0, so it goes out as an object.

The manual's own json_encode example shows it: after unset($sequential[1]), the array ["foo","bar","baz","blong"] encodes as {"0":"foo","2":"baz","3":"blong"}.


Remove one item from a PHP list and json_encode stops sending a list.

<?php
$tags = ['php', 'typescript', 'go'];

$kept = array_filter($tags, fn ($t) => $t !== 'php');
echo json_encode($kept), PHP_EOL;
// keys 1 and 2 survive: a JSON object, not an array

echo json_encode(array_values($kept)), PHP_EOL;
// keys reset to 0 and 1: a JSON array

The nasty part is that the shape depends on the data. Filter out 'go' instead and keys 0 and 1 remain, which is still a list, so you get an array. Your TypeScript client calls data.tags.map(...), it works for weeks, and then one request drops the first element and the call throws a TypeError, because a plain object has no map method.

It runs the other way too. The json_encode page shows that an empty array encodes as [], so a PHP map that happens to be empty reaches the client as an array, not {}. JSON_FORCE_OBJECT exists, but it is a blunt switch: the same example turns a nested list [[1,2,3]] into {"0":{"0":1,"1":2,"2":3}}.

Fix it on the PHP side

Treat the JSON shape as part of the API contract and make it explicit.

For lists, call array_values after anything that can leave gaps: array_filter, unset, array_unique. The array_filter manual page points to it for exactly this. On PHP 8.1+, array_is_list checks whether keys are "consecutive numbers from 0 to count($array)-1", which makes a cheap assertion in a response test.

For maps where order matters, stop sending a JSON object. Send a list of records:

<?php
$options = [
    10 => 'Express',
    2 => 'Standard',
    'pickup' => 'Store pickup',
];

$payload = [];
foreach ($options as $id => $label) {
    $payload[] = ['id' => (string) $id, 'label' => $label];
}

echo json_encode($payload), PHP_EOL;
// a JSON array of {id, label} objects, Express first

The (string) cast matters. PHP already turned '10' into int 10, so without it id is a JSON number for numeric keys and a string for 'pickup'. Your TypeScript type would have to be number | string. Cast once on the server and the client gets one type.

Fix it on the TypeScript side

Type the payload as the list it is, and build a Map if you need lookups by ID. MDN states that a Map "remembers the original insertion order of the keys", and that holds for "10" and "2" as much as for "pickup":

type ShippingOption = { id: string; label: string };

async function loadOptions(): Promise<Map<string, string>> {
  const res = await fetch('/api/shipping-options');
  const list = (await res.json()) as ShippingOption[];
  return new Map(list.map((o) => [o.id, o.label]));
}

The same MDN page is blunt about plain objects: their order "is complex. As a result, it's best not to rely on property order." Use objects for lookup and arrays or Maps for anything a user sees in sequence.

When you don't own the PHP side and the list-or-object flip is already in production, normalise at the boundary:

function asList<T>(value: unknown): T[] {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value as T[];
  if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') {
    return Object.values(value) as T[];
  }
  throw new TypeError('expected a list or an object');
}

This is safe for the array_filter case: the surviving keys were already ascending, so the ascending integer order of Object.values matches the original list. It cannot rescue the shipping dropdown. Once JSON.parse turns a map with integer keys inserted out of order into a JavaScript object, the order is gone. Short of parsing the raw response text yourself, only a change to the payload brings it back.

If this was useful

PHP arrays do the work of lists, maps and ordered maps all at once, and both bugs in this post come from that one structure being split into three on the TypeScript side. PHP to TypeScript walks through that split for PHP 8+ developers: when the data is an array, a Map, a Record or a tuple, and how to keep the JSON contract between the two honest.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you came from PHP, start with PHP to TypeScript, then go to The TypeScript Type System when you want the deep end. Books 1 and 2 are the core path for everyone else, and TypeScript in Production is for the day you ship it at work.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop Is Coming in 27.04 - And It Kills sudo apt (But Maybe That Is the Point?)
articles.description: I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.  Not a new wallpaper...
articles.body_html:
I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.

Not a new wallpaper kind of change. More like, you will not be able to install things the way you do now.

Canonical has restarted work on Ubuntu Core Desktop. It is a locked down, all-snap version of Ubuntu. And they want it to become the default Ubuntu. They already call the Ubuntu we use today "Classic Ubuntu." That name kind of gives it away, no? :)

Are we supposed to panic? I don't think so. But I do think we should look at it honestly before it lands in 27.04, which is about 6 months away.

So I went through the details. I am Taqui, I build web apps with Next.js and TypeScript, mostly full-stack stuff. One of my side projects is Wryte, a small AI blog writer I made for myself. So I read announcements like this with a normal user hat on, not an admin hat. Here is what I found.

Quick background

Ubuntu Core is not new. Canonical made it in 2015 for IoT, robots and industrial devices. Stuff you install once and never touch again. It worked well there.

Desktop was different. In 2023 they showed a first preview of Core Desktop. It was supposed to come in 2024, then it went quiet for 2 years.

Why? Their engineering chief John Seager said the preview was not good enough. They put almost the whole desktop in one giant base snap. That makes updates huge and swapping parts very hard.

That is just bad engineering, I guess they were in a hurry to show something.

Now a new team is splitting it into small pieces. Daily builds in the next few weeks.

Canonical actually posted the official announcement on Discourse here: Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop. It calls Core Desktop the most fundamental shift in Ubuntu desktop architecture so far. That post is where they explain the new split snap design.

How does it work

On normal Ubuntu, sudo apt update writes directly into your system folders. The OS changes itself.

On Core Desktop, the system is immutable. Read-only. That means the core cannot be broken by a bad package.

Think Lego, not like a recipe. There are 6 main blocks:

  1. gadget snap - bootloader, partitions, TPM encryption
  2. kernel snap - kernel and drivers
  3. boot base - minimal root filesystem
  4. snapd - updates and rollback
  5. system snaps - wifi, bluetooth, audio, power
  6. desktop and app snaps - GNOME / KDE and every app you install

Each snap is a compressed read-only file. Your home folder is separate and writable. If an update breaks, it rolls back on reboot.

Source: Inside Ubuntu Core docs

What I like about this is it is simple to explain. Want to update network without touching kernel? You can. That part makes sense to me.

How is this different from Fedora Silverblue

Silverblue and NixOS already do immutable stuff. But they are not beginner friendly. You have to learn RPM-OSTree, image layering, wikis, etc. Just to install something.

Core Desktop is trying to do the same thing, but with snaps, which Ubuntu users already know. So install feels familiar. That is the whole point, I think. Less learning curve.

So you cannot apt install?

Yes. That is the big one.

No sudo apt install on the host. No .deb packages on the base. No flatpak on the host either.

If it is not in the Snap Store, you are stuck. Even Canonical says this is the biggest problem right now.

So they are pushing three use cases for 27.04:

1. Browser focused PCs
Firefox and Chromium already work as snaps. Most of us live in the browser anyway, so for a lot of people this might already be enough.

2. Developer PCs
If the host is read-only, how do you code? Canonical says use containers. With LXD, Docker or their Workshop tool you can run a container in one command and inside you can apt install anything. Your app still shows on the desktop.

This part feels familiar to me, since I ship Next.js apps from a containerised setup myself sometimes. I get why they do it. It just does not feel as normal as installing directly. Not yet, at least.

3. Gaming PCs
They spent over a year on the Steam snap, with Proton and Mesa drivers inside. For Nvidia, there is a new gpu-2604 interface to deliver drivers via snaps.

Also, because kernel is a snap, you could switch to a gaming kernel in one command. That would be cool if it works.

And flavors? GNOME is not the only one. KDE, Budgie, MATE can all be swapped because the desktop is separate from the base. Canonical is already working with KDE on KDE Neon Core. Each snap has stable, candidate, beta, edge channels, so you could keep the base stable and test desktop on edge. That part I actually like :)

What happens to Classic Ubuntu

They say Classic Ubuntu is not going away yet. There is still a Debian team maintaining debs.

But John Seager also said his long term plan is to make Core the default for desktop, server and edge. For companies and governments that makes a lot of sense. They can deploy thousands of identical locked machines with up to 15 years support.

If that is where the money is, and best engineers move there, I think Classic will slowly fade. That is how Ubuntu has always moved - enterprise first, desktop follows.

My worry

For enterprise this is great. For people who like to tinker, it puts a wall between you and the machine.

One tester tried Core Desktop on a Steam Deck. Battery was bad, he wanted TLP and to edit a systemd file. On normal Ubuntu that is 10 seconds. On Core he was locked out.

Another tester, William, said the installer forced Ubuntu One login and TPM encryption. No choice. Once you are in, you cannot unsnap the OS or install debs on host. He said it felt more closed than Windows.

I get it. When everything is read-only, that Linux tinkering spirit goes away a bit. That is the part that worries me.

I am someone who sets up my PC once, installs my main apps, and never changes anything. For me, tiny updates that never break sound perfect. In theory it sounds great.

But I also started with Ubuntu because I could open a terminal and fix things myself. That freedom mattered.

Final thoughts

Core Desktop is not replacing Classic tomorrow. But the direction is clear. Canonical wants immutable, snap-first, enterprise-shaped. That is their future.

I do not know if it is good or bad yet. We will know when we actually try it.

So what do you think? Are you staying for this, or are you already packing for Debian or Mint? :)

If you want to read more, the Inside Ubuntu Core docs are actually readable, even for desktop users. And the official Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop thread on Ubuntu Discourse is the best place to follow daily builds. Worth a look :)

I'm Taqui, full-stack dev from India building web products with Next.js and TypeScript. I post what I'm learning here and on my portfolio at taqui.in. If this helped, say hi in the comments :)

articles.title: Running an NVIDIA DLSS Neural-Rendering Pipeline on Apple Silicon
articles.description: Hey everyone!  So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which attempted to port NVIDIA's DLSS 5 technology to macOS using the MLX backend.

I was genuinely disappointed when I saw the performance numbers: 6 FPS, and that too on a pre-rendered video with just a single pass. 💀

So I decided to experiment with it myself.

Before going further, I should mention that I did take partial help from a coding agent, mainly for testing and analysis. The actual coding and implementation work was done by me.

Anyway, here's what I ended up doing.

I ported the project into OBS Studio as a plugin, extracted the model weights from nvngx_dlssnr.dll (the main Windows DLSS 5 neural-rendering DLL provided by NVIDIA), and started engineering a different, hybrid backend.

The idea was to distribute the workload across Apple's available hardware rather than relying entirely on GPU inference.

Here's how my current pipeline works:

Apple Neural Engine (ANE) via Core ML: Handles the main deep-learning transformer inference passes using the 31 HT and 71 HT models.

MLX: Handles AI upscaling and experimental frame generation.

Temporal stability: I've implemented temporal stabilization to reduce texture flickering and RGB poisoning.

A small warning about frame generation: it's still experimental, partially implemented, and quite buggy. I'm actively working on improving it.

The good news is that temporal stability has improved significantly. Texture flickering is much less noticeable, and RGB poisoning has been reduced by a huge margin compared to my earlier tests.

How am I feeding frames into the pipeline?

Right now, I'm using a PS5 connected to my Mac through an HDMI capture card, with the captured frames being processed through OBS Studio.

However, the pipeline isn't limited to PS5 footage. It can process other OBS video sources as well.

The three rendering modes

I've implemented three different modes: Fidelity, Balanced, and Performance.

  1. Fidelity Mode

This is the heaviest configuration.

It uses a double 71 HT transformer pass, prioritizing neural-rendering quality over performance.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 8–11 FPS

With frame generation: ~35 FPS

It looks impressive, but as mentioned earlier, frame generation is still experimental and can introduce visual artifacts and instability.

  1. Balanced Mode

This one is particularly interesting.

Instead of running the same model twice, Balanced uses a heterogeneous pipeline, with the first pass running the 31 HT model and the second pass running the 71 HT model.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 12.5–15 FPS

With frame generation: 45–48 FPS

It's basically my attempt to combine the advantages of both models without going all-in on the heavier double-71 configuration.

  1. Performance Mode

This is the lightweight configuration.

It runs a single 31 HT transformer pass.

Current results:

Without frame generation: ~20 FPS

With frame generation: 70–80 FPS

Obviously, there's a trade-off in rendering quality compared to Fidelity, but this mode provides considerably better performance.

Again, the frame-generated numbers shouldn't be confused with native inference performance. FG is still a work in progress, and visual stability isn't completely solved yet.

How am I even getting double-digit FPS?

Now, you might be wondering how I went from the original project's 6 FPS on a pre-rendered video to these numbers.

Well, I changed quite a few things in the original approach.

(A) The 480p neural-inference trick

Instead of directly feeding full 1080p frames into the neural inference backend, I do something different.

First, I capture the console output at 1080p through the HDMI capture card.

Then I downscale the frames to 480p before feeding them into the neural-rendering backend.

Once neural inference is complete, I upscale the output back to 1080p using an MLX-based AI upscaler.

The idea is to reduce the computational cost of inference while using AI upscaling to reconstruct and preserve details that conventional spatial or temporal upscaling might soften.

In some scenes, the resulting details can even appear better than the original input.

Of course, this approach has its own limitations, but the performance improvement has been pretty substantial.

(B) Moving neural inference from MLX to the ANE

This was another major change.

The original project relied on MLX for GPU-based neural inference.

Instead of following the same approach, I moved major parts of the deep-learning network onto Apple's Neural Engine through Core ML.

Think of it this way:

On NVIDIA GPUs, you have dedicated Tensor Cores for accelerating certain AI workloads.

On Apple Silicon, you have the Apple Neural Engine, which provides dedicated hardware acceleration for supported machine-learning operations.

They're not architecturally identical, obviously, but the general idea is to take advantage of dedicated neural acceleration hardware.

My goal was to avoid putting all the inference pressure on the GPU, especially since the GPU is already doing other work.

MLX is still useful, and newer Apple GPU architectures, particularly the M5 series and beyond, may offer additional advantages for GPU-based machine learning.

But for my M4 Pro, using Core ML to leverage the ANE for the main transformer inference stages made much more sense for this particular workload.

So instead of having MLX handle everything, I ended up with a heterogeneous backend where Core ML/ANE and MLX handle different parts of the pipeline.

Other things I've implemented

I've also recreated a RenoDX/OptiScaler-style configuration menu for DLSS 5, allowing users to tweak different model and pipeline settings.

Alongside that, I've implemented an RTSS-style performance metrics overlay to monitor performance while the pipeline is running.

These are still evolving, just like the rest of the project.

What's next?

The biggest thing I'm working on right now is frame-generation stability.

Temporal stabilization has already helped reduce flickering and RGB artifacts significantly in the normal neural-rendering pipeline, but enabling frame generation can still reintroduce some of those issues.

So that's my current priority.

The project is very much experimental, and there's still a lot of testing, optimization, and debugging left to do.

But considering where the original experiment started, I'm pretty happy with the progress so far.

Feel free to check it out, give it a try, and share your feedback!

I'm particularly interested in hearing from people working with Apple Silicon, Core ML, MLX, Metal, neural rendering, or similar graphics pipelines.

articles.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
articles.description: string.Format reparses its template on every call. CompositeFormat parses it once, and the allocation drop is not subtle.
articles.body_html:
I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed.

The template gets reparsed every time

When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times.

CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. The holes are already located. The call just fills them.

const string Template = "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}";

// Parsed once, up front.
var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse(Template);

// Later, in the hot loop:
string a = string.Format(ci, Template, id, when, amount);   // reparses Template
string b = string.Format(ci, parsed,   id, when, amount);   // reuses the parse

So I counted. I formatted the same CSV line five million times through each path, best of five rounds, summing the line lengths so the compiler couldn't throw the work away, and tracking allocations with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread.

const int Iterations = 5_000_000;
var when = new DateTime(2026, 11, 7, 8, 11, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc);
const decimal amount = 1234.56m;
var ci = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse("{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}");

long sinkA = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkA += string.Format(ci, "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}", i, when, amount).Length;

long sinkB = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkB += string.Format(ci, parsed, i, when, amount).Length;

Here's what came back:

Runtime: .NET 10.0.14
5,000,000 formats, best of 5

  string.Format(string)            837.9 ms    167.6 ns/call    838.5 MB
  string.Format(CompositeFormat)   517.7 ms    103.5 ns/call    457.0 MB

The time ratio bounced between about 1.4x and 1.6x depending on the round, which is honest for a microbenchmark running in a container I don't fully control. I care about the ratio, not the absolute milliseconds. But the allocation number didn't bounce at all: string.Format(string) churned 838.5 MB, the CompositeFormat path 457.0 MB. That's a steady 381 MB of garbage I was handing the GC for no reason other than relocating the same three braces over and over. Both paths produced byte-identical output, which is the whole point. Same answer, less work.

The allocation gap is the part worth sitting with. The reparsing doesn't just cost CPU; it allocates on the way through, and that allocation is what eventually turns into GC pauses in a service that's doing this constantly. Cutting it nearly in half for a one-line change is a good trade.

When this is a waste of time

Here's the caveat, and it's a real one: CompositeFormat only pays off when you reuse the same template a lot. If you're formatting a string once, or a handful of times, parsing it into a CompositeFormat first is strictly more work than just calling string.Format with the literal. You've added an allocation and a line of code to save nothing. This is a hot-path tool. A log line formatted per-request, a CSV row per record, a template rendered in a tight loop — those are where it earns its keep. The welcome email you send once? Leave it alone.

My honest opinion: for most code, interpolated strings ($"{id},{when:yyyy-MM-dd}") are already the right default, and the compiler handles them well. CompositeFormat isn't competing with those. It's for the specific case where your template lives in a variable or a resource file, gets reused heavily, and you were reaching for string.Format anyway. In that narrow spot it's close to free to adopt. The one gotcha: CompositeFormat.Parse validates the template up front, so a malformed template throws at parse time instead of at the first format call. I'd call that a feature.

The thing I like about it is how little it asks. You're not rewriting the formatting, not switching APIs, not learning a new builder. You pull the parse out of the loop. One line moves up, and a few hundred megabytes of garbage stop existing. That's the kind of change I'll take every time.

Have you found a spot in your own code where the template was constant but you were paying to rediscover it? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking the things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
articles.description: A tiny endpoint was allocating like crazy. The culprit was a fresh JsonSerializerOptions built inside the handler on every request. Here's the measured cost and the one-line fix.
articles.body_html:
A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return.

Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler:

var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
});

Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug.

What the options object actually is

I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. The first time you serialize with a given options instance, System.Text.Json walks your type with reflection, builds the metadata it needs to write it (the contract for Order, for Line, the converters, the property names), caches all of that on that options instance, and then freezes the instance so it can't change underneath the cache. That setup is not cheap, and it's the reason the reused path is fast: you pay once, then every serialize after that rides the warm cache.

Build a new options object every call and you throw that cache away every call. Fresh reflection, fresh contracts, fresh everything, two hundred thousand times. You're not configuring a serializer. You're constructing one from scratch in your hot path.

Making it admit the cost

I didn't want to argue from a profiler's hunch, so I ran both shapes side by side. Same order, same settings, serialized 200,000 times. One path news up the options each iteration. The other builds it once and reuses it. I measured wall time and total allocated bytes for each. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio far more than the raw milliseconds.

static JsonSerializerOptions BuildOptions() => new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

var cached = BuildOptions();

// warm both paths' first-use cost before timing
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, BuildOptions());

// Path A: a brand-new options object on every call
var before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
{
    var opts = BuildOptions();
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, opts);
}
sw.Stop();
var aMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var aAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

// Path B: one cached instance, reused
before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
sw.Restart();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
sw.Stop();
var bMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var bAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

The order itself is nothing special — a record with an enum status and a list of three lines, the kind of thing any API hands back:

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, OrderStatus Status, List<Line> Lines);
record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }

Here's what printed, on .NET 10, Release build:

Serializing the same order 200,000 times.

new options each call : 17,402.5 ms    7,021.9 MB
one cached instance   :    146.0 ms      166.3 MB

time   : ~120x slower when rebuilt each call
memory :  ~42x more allocated

A hundred and twenty times slower. Seven gigabytes of allocation to produce the exact same JSON string that the cached path produced in a hundred and sixty-six megabytes. I ran it twice to be sure the numbers held, and they did, within a few percent. That's not a tuning opportunity. That's a serializer rebuilding its entire type model, over and over, for no reason.

The fix is embarrassingly small

Move the options out of the method. Build it once, hang it off a static field, reuse it forever.

static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOpts = new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

// in the handler
var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, JsonOpts);

That's the entire change. The instance is immutable once it's been used anyway, so sharing it across every request and every thread is exactly what it's built for — JsonSerializer reads from a frozen options object concurrently without complaint.

If your settings really do vary per call, and sometimes they genuinely do, don't fall back to newing one up each time. Cache the handful of variants you actually use, keyed by whatever differs. In practice most codebases have two or three distinct option sets total, not one per request. And if you're on the default settings with no customization at all, JsonSerializer.Serialize(order) already uses a cached internal instance, so the parameterless call was never the problem — it's specifically the configured-options-inline pattern that bites.

One honest caveat on the number: 120x is what this payload and this machine gave me. A bigger, deeper object graph makes the per-call rebuild even more lopsided because there's more metadata to reconstruct. A trivial payload narrows the gap. But I've never seen reuse lose, and the allocation story is one-directional regardless — a fresh options object is always garbage you didn't need to make.

I keep finding these in code reviews now that I know the shape. Any new JsonSerializerOptions that isn't assigned to a static readonly field is worth a second look. Nine times out of ten it's sitting in a method that runs a lot.

Where's yours hiding? Drop a line if you find one in a hot path — I'd bet money it's in a serialization helper somebody wrote once and never profiled.
